title: Light and Diurnal Cycle Affect Human Heart Rate: Possible Role for the Circadian Pacemaker
research_question: To investigate how light input to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) affects human heart rate, considering different phases of the day-night cycle and varying light intensities.

participants.description: Experiment 1: 11 males (22-40 years) and 6 females (22-32 years). Experiment 2: 10 males (23-38 years). All volunteers were students and collaborators from the institute in the Netherlands, healthy, with regular working weeks. Two subjects in Experiment 1 were light smokers; none in Experiment 2.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Experiment 1: Participants were exposed to '0 lux' (complete darkness, dark cap over eyes, eyes closed) for 20 minutes, followed by 'indoor light' (daylight supplemented with artificial light, unmeasured illumination level at home, or 150 lux tube lighting at the institute) for 10 minutes. These conditions were applied at 7 different Zeitgeber Times (ZT0, ZT4, ZT8, ZT12, ZT16, ZT20, ZT24) over a 24-hour cycle.

Experiment 2: Participants were exposed to '0 lux' (dark cap, diffuse filter, light visor off, eyes closed) for 20 minutes, followed by '100 lux' (light visor with diffuse filter and extra gray filter) for 10 minutes, and then '800 lux' (light visor with diffuse filter, maximum capacity) for 10 minutes. Light was generated by a portable light visor (MediluX BV) at eye distance (6-8 cm). These conditions were applied at 5 different Zeitgeber Times (ZT0, ZT8, ZT15, ZT20, ZT24) over a 24-hour cycle.

mechanisms: The SCN modulates heart rate via (multisynaptic) neural pathways.
Light influences the output of the SCN to the pineal, adrenal, and autonomic nervous system.
The increase in human heart rate by light is mediated by the SCN, as supported by the similarity of the observed phase response curve (PRC) to other SCN-mediated responses.
The effect of light on heart rate is dose-dependent, further supporting SCN mediation.
The visual cortex probably does not mediate the effect of light on heart rate, as indicated by the dose-dependency and diffuse light exposure.
The proposed pathway for light's effect on HR is via the retinohypothalamic tract to the SCN, and from the SCN via the paraventricular nucleus, brain stem, and spinal cord to the heart.
implementation_implications: The experimental setup could be used to investigate the effect of changes in the circadian pacemaker on the response of resting HR to light and diurnal phase in patients with hypertension, which may help understand the role of circadian disturbances in hypertension.

limitations: In Experiment 1, the indoor light intensity was not controlled or equal across different Zeitgeber Times, which limited conclusions regarding a diurnal rhythm in sensitivity of HR to light stimulation.
While strong evidence is provided, the study does not directly prove SCN mediation of HR in humans.
The study cannot completely exclude a role of a phase response curve (PRC) in retinal sensitivity for the observed increase in HR to light.

paper_metadata.title: Light and Diurnal Cycle Affect Human Heart Rate: Possible Role for the Circadian Pacemaker
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Light and Diurnal Cycle Affect Human Heart Rate: Possible Role for the Circadian Pacemaker
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Humans and animals demonstrate diurnal rhythms in physiology and behavior, which are generated by the circadian pacemaker, located in the supra-chiasmatic nucleus (SCN). The endogenous diurnal rhythm of the SCN is synchronized to the diurnal cycle most effectively by light. However, light also influences the SCN and its output instantaneously, as is demonstrated for the immediate effects of light on SCN neuronal firing frequency and on the output of the SCN to the pineal, inhibiting melatonin secretion. In addition to this, the circadian pacemaker modulates neuronally also other organs such as the adrenal. Therefore, the authors investigated the effect of this light input to the SCN on human heart rate, using light at different phases of the day-night cycle and light of different intensities. Resting heart rate (HR) was measured in volunteers between 20 and 40 years of age during supine, awake, resting conditions, and after 2 hours of fasting. In Experiment 1, HR was measured at different times over the day-night cycle at 0 lux and at indoor light. In Experiment 2, HR was measured at different times over the day-night cycle at controlled light intensities of 0 lux, 100 lux, and 800 lux. The authors demonstrate a clear diurnal rhythm in resting HR in complete darkness, similar to that measured under constant routine conditions. Second, it is demonstrated that light increases resting HR depending on the phase of the day-night cycle and on the intensity of light. These data strongly suggest that the circadian pacemaker modulates human HR.

environmental_features: light exposure (e.g., 0 lux, other controlled light conditions)
diurnal cycle (measurements at specific Zeitgeber times: ZT0, ZT4, ZT8, ZT12, ZT16, ZT20, ZT24)
control_conditions: constant routine protocol (to isolate endogenous circadian rhythm)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The human endogenous circadian pacemaker plays a role in regulating heart rate, potentially independently of direct light effects.

mechanism_chain.description: Light and the diurnal cycle entrain the endogenous circadian pacemaker, which in turn physiologically modulates human heart rate.
